title: UTF-8 Validation
description: Brute force to optimized: hardcoded pattern comparisons versus a uniform leading bit count.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Given an array of integers representing byte values (each between 0 and 255), determine whether it represents a valid sequence of UTF-8 encoded characters. A valid character is encoded using 1 to 4 bytes: a 1 byte character starts with a 0 bit, and a multi byte character starts with as many leading 1 bits as its total byte count followed by a 0, with every following continuation byte starting with the bit pattern 10.

blocks.caption: The leading bits of the first byte announce how many bytes this character spans

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Given an array of integers representing byte values (each between 0 and 255), determine whether it represents a valid sequence of UTF-8 encoded characters. A valid character is encoded using 1 to 4 bytes: a 1 byte character starts with a 0 bit, and a multi byte character starts with as many leading 1 bits as its total byte count followed by a 0, with every following continuation byte starting with the bit pattern 10.

blocks.title: Analogy: Checking Envelope Prefixes for a Valid Multi Part Package
blocks.text: Like inspecting a stack of package labels where each label's prefix announces how many follow-up parts belong with it, and every announced follow-up part must actually be present and correctly marked as a continuation.

blocks.caption: The leading bits of the first byte announce how many bytes this character spans

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: data = [197, 130, 1]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["197 is 11000101, starting with 110, announcing a 2 byte character","130 is 10000010, a valid continuation byte","The leading 110 pattern promises exactly one continuation byte, and 130's own leading 10 pattern fulfills that promise"],["1 is 00000001, a valid standalone 1 byte character","no more bytes expected","A leading 0 bit means this byte is a complete character on its own, requiring no continuation bytes"],["Answer","true","Every byte in the sequence is accounted for by a correctly formed character, with nothing left over or missing"]]}

blocks.text: Example: data = [235, 140, 4]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["235 is 11101011, starting with 1110, announcing a 3 byte character needing 2 continuation bytes","140 is 10001100, a valid continuation byte","The first continuation byte correctly starts with 10, matching what a 3-byte character's second byte must look like"],["4 is 00000100, which does NOT start with 10","this is not a valid continuation byte","The second promised continuation byte instead looks like a brand new standalone character, breaking the announced structure"],["Answer","false","A promised continuation byte failed to match the required 10 prefix, so the sequence is invalid"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: a single byte like [65]
65 is 01000001, starting with a single 0 bit, a completely valid standalone 1 byte character, giving true.
5. How Should We Think?

Before writing any comparisons, notice that this problem is really two nested questions asked repeatedly: "how many bytes does this character claim to span", and "do the following bytes actually honor that claim".

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The first byte of every character encodes its own byte count directly in its leading bits: a single 0 means 1 byte, and a run of k leading 1 bits (for k from 2 to 4) followed by a 0 means a k-byte character.

Observation 2: Once that byte count is known, the rest of the check is completely mechanical: exactly (byte count minus 1) further bytes must each independently start with the fixed 10 prefix, nothing more is needed to confirm the character is well-formed.

Observation 3: Explicitly listing 4 separate hardcoded bit patterns (0, 110, 1110, 11110) works, but it hides a simpler uniform rule underneath: the leading byte's 1-bit count IS the byte count, directly, with no lookup table required.

Observation 4: Counting leading 1 bits is itself just a small bitwise loop, checking the top bit, shifting a mask, and stopping the moment a 0 bit is found, replacing 4 separate comparisons with one small counting loop that works uniformly for every case.

Whenever a problem presents several fixed-length bit-pattern cases that all follow the same underlying structure, look for the single counting or arithmetic rule that generates all of them, instead of hardcoding each case separately.

This problem also tests careful bounds and index tracking as much as bit manipulation itself, since consuming a variable number of bytes per character means the scan must always verify enough bytes actually remain before reading them.
6. Brute Force Solution

At the start of each character, compare its leading bits against each of the known valid patterns individually (0 for 1 byte, 110 for 2 byte, 1110 for 3 byte, 11110 for 4 byte) using a chain of explicit comparisons, then verify the correct number of continuation bytes follow, each checked against the 10 pattern individually.
Step by step algorithm

items: At the current byte, compare its top bits against each known valid leading pattern in turn.
Based on which pattern matches, determine how many continuation bytes should follow.
Check each expected continuation byte individually against the 10 pattern.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The four leading-pattern checks are ordered from the most specific mask to correctly distinguish a 1 byte character (top bit 0) from a 2, 3, or 4 byte leading byte, each requiring progressively more leading 1 bits before a 0.
i + num_bytes > n is checked before reading any continuation bytes, preventing an out-of-bounds read when a character is announced but the array ends too soon.
The inner loop over continuation bytes starts at k = 1, not k = 0, since index i itself is the already-classified leading byte, and only the bytes after it need the 10-prefix check.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every character's leading pattern is correctly matched against the 4 valid options, and every required continuation byte is verified, so this correctly validates the sequence.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass through the bytes.
Space: O(1) extra, no additional structure is used.

Limitation: comparing against 4 separate hardcoded bit patterns is more special casing than necessary, when the number of leading 1 bits directly and uniformly determines the byte count without needing 4 separate comparisons.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Unlike many bit manipulation problems, this one's brute force is already O(n) time and O(1) space, so there is no asymptotic bottleneck to chase here. What is worth improving is the amount of hardcoded special-casing: 4 separate mask comparisons, each paired with a specific expected pattern, are really testing the same underlying fact four different ways, how many leading 1 bits appear before the first 0. Counting that run of 1 bits directly, with a small loop that shifts a single bit mask rightward and stops at the first 0, produces the exact same byte count without needing to remember or re-derive four separate bit patterns. This is a genuine simplification: fewer special cases to get wrong, and the same logic now naturally rejects any leading byte with more than 4 leading 1 bits or exactly 1, without a fifth explicit comparison.

Count the number of consecutive leading 1 bits in the first byte directly, by shifting and checking from the most significant bit downward. This count directly gives the total number of bytes the character should span: 0 leading 1 bits means a 1 byte character, 2 means a 2 byte character, 3 means 3 bytes, and 4 means 4 bytes. A leading 1 bit count of exactly 1, or more than 4, is immediately invalid. Then verify that many continuation bytes follow, each checked against the 10 prefix pattern.
9. Optimized Solution
Count the leading 1 bits directly to determine the byte count, uniformly, without separate hardcoded comparisons.
Dry run for the first byte of data = [235, 140, 4], 235 = 11101011

blocks.caption: Optimized: count leading 1 bits directly to get the byte count, no hardcoded pattern list needed

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), the same single pass, now with a uniform leading bit count instead of separate comparisons.
Space: O(1) extra.
Why This Works

A byte's leading 1-bit run length and its role in UTF-8 encoding are literally the same piece of information stated two different ways: the standard defines a k-byte character's first byte as k leading 1 bits followed by a 0, so counting those bits directly recovers k without needing a separate named pattern for each value of k.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Leading 1-bit count","Meaning"],"rows":[["0","A 1-byte character; the byte starts directly with a 0 bit"],["2, 3, or 4","A multi-byte character of that many total bytes"],["1, or more than 4","Always invalid; UTF-8 defines no such leading byte shape"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: mask starts at 0b10000000, the very first (most significant) bit position, and is shifted right by one after each check, sweeping across the byte from most significant to least significant.
The while byte & mask loop increments num_bytes once per leading 1 bit found, and stops naturally the instant a 0 bit is reached, without needing an explicit bit-position counter variable.
if num_bytes < 2 or num_bytes > 4 rejects both a lone stray 1 bit (which is not a valid leading pattern on its own) and any run longer than the 4-byte maximum UTF-8 actually defines.
The rest of the function, the bounds check and the continuation-byte loop, is unchanged from the brute force, since only the leading-byte classification step actually needed simplifying.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

This problem rewards recognizing the uniform underlying rule (leading 1 bit count directly equals byte count) behind what looks like 4 separate special cases, which reduces the amount of hardcoded pattern matching needed and makes the logic easier to verify as correct.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting to reject a leading 1 bit count of exactly 1, which is never a valid UTF-8 leading byte pattern on its own, since a 1-byte character must start with a plain 0 bit, not a single 1 followed by a 0.
Not checking that enough bytes actually remain in the array before reading the expected number of continuation bytes, risking an out of bounds read or array index error.

Checking a continuation byte's full value against a fixed constant instead of masking first: only the top two bits of a continuation byte matter, so comparing without masking away the lower six bits would reject otherwise-valid continuation bytes.

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["A byte sequence that ends in the middle of a multi-byte character","Too few continuation bytes remain, so the bounds check must catch this before an out-of-bounds read occurs"],["A leading byte announcing more than 4 total bytes","Always invalid regardless of what follows, since UTF-8 defines no character longer than 4 bytes"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explain the leading bit count rule explicitly (the number of leading 1 bits in the first byte is exactly the total byte count for that character) since this single sentence replaces the need to memorize 4 separate bit patterns.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Several fixed bit-pattern cases that all look similar" points toward looking for the single counting or arithmetic rule that generates every case uniformly, instead of hardcoding each pattern as a separate comparison.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you validate a UTF-8 encoded byte stream, where bytes arrive one at a time rather than all at once? Track the remaining expected continuation byte count as persistent state between calls instead of using a single self-contained loop.

What is the maximum and minimum number of bytes this algorithm could scan before returning false? It can fail as early as the very first byte, an invalid leading pattern, or as late as the last byte of a well-formed-looking sequence that runs out of continuation bytes.

Could this be solved without any bitwise operators at all? Yes, by converting each integer to its binary string representation and using string prefix checks instead, though this trades simplicity of implementation for a slower, more allocation-heavy solution.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Same "leading marker byte announces how many follow" structure as variable-length integer encodings used in many binary file formats and network protocols.
Same "replace several hardcoded bit-pattern comparisons with one uniform counting rule" insight as recognizing the bit-trie family's preference for counting bits directly instead of table lookups.
Same careful bounds-checking discipline as any variable-stride array scan, such as run-length decoding or multi-byte character iteration in general.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time, O(1) space.
Optimized: O(n) time, O(1) space, using a uniform leading bit count instead of separate hardcoded comparisons.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Leading-bit-count-driven variable-length byte sequence validation
Core Idea: The number of leading 1 bits in a character's first byte directly equals its total byte count, replacing 4 separate hardcoded patterns with one counting rule
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: What looks like 4 separate special cases is really one uniform rule, counting the leading 1 bits, applied 4 different ways
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Count the leading 1s, that is the byte count
